lines: A reader opens a snapshot, and then the same row gets updated four more times while that reader stays open.
Does any one of those four now-dead versions ever become reclaimable while the reader is still sitting there, open?
answer: For as long as that reader stays open, none of them can be reclaimed.

lines: Run it for real: not one of the four dead versions came back reclaimable while the reader stayed open.
A long-lived reader blocks reclaim of everything newer than it, not only the one version it actually reads.
That same reader now closes instead, on the identical workload.
Do those same four now-dead versions become reclaimable once it's gone?
answer: Closing the reader frees every single one.

lines: Run it for real: closing that reader genuinely freed every one of its previously-pinned dead versions.
steps.takeaway: A version becomes reclaimable once no open snapshot could still need it; closing a reader removes exactly that need.

lines: Run the identical workload twice: once with that reader staying open the entire time, once with it closing early instead.
Does the long-lived run genuinely retain more versions than the short-lived one?
answer: The long-lived run retains far more.

lines: Run it for real: the long-lived run genuinely retained far more versions than the short-lived run, on the identical workload.
steps.takeaway: One long-running reader turns into a real, measurable storage-growth problem, on a workload that would otherwise stay small.

lines: One real production system's own documentation states this exact coupling directly.
Does it name actually ending a long-running open transaction as something that frees up space its own cleanup process alone cannot?
answer: It tells administrators to end those transactions directly.

lines: That system's own documentation states it in exactly those words: end long-running open transactions directly, found by checking for backends whose own transaction age has grown large.
steps.takeaway: The real fix for this isn't a smarter cleanup pass; it's ending the long-running transaction that's pinning the horizon.

lines: That same system's own documentation also names exactly what that horizon is made of.
A backend's own value in that system's own activity view is named directly as that backend's own xmin horizon.
So here's the shape of this whole topic: a version becomes reclaimable only once no open snapshot could possibly still need it, never any sooner.

One long-running reader genuinely blocks every single reclaim newer than it, not just the one version it directly reads, which is exactly why it turns into a real, measurable storage-growth problem on a workload that would otherwise stay small.
The actual fix for that isn't a smarter cleanup pass running more often; it's ending the long-running transaction that's pinning the horizon in the first place.
